facts.title: The most famous painting in the world
facts.statement: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre. Its global fame dates largely from its theft in 1911, which put it on front pages worldwide.
facts.question: Which painting by Leonardo da Vinci hangs in the Louvre and is the world's most famous portrait?
facts.hook: It became the most famous painting on Earth because somebody stole it.

facts.title: The swirling night sky
facts.statement: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889 from his room at an asylum in Saint-Rémy, working from memory and imagination.
facts.question: Which Van Gogh painting shows a swirling night sky over a village?

facts.title: The face of anxiety
facts.statement: Edvard Munch's The Scream exists in four versions and depicts a figure under a blood-red sky that Munch said he saw over Oslo.
facts.question: Which Edvard Munch work shows a figure holding its face under a red sky?

facts.title: The painting against war
facts.statement: Picasso's Guernica, painted in 1937, depicts the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War and became the definitive anti-war painting.
facts.question: Which Picasso mural depicts the bombing of a Basque town in 1937?

facts.title: The melting clocks
facts.statement: Salvador Dalí's The Persistence of Memory, with its drooping pocket watches, is the best-known image of Surrealism.
facts.question: Which Dalí painting features melting clocks?

facts.title: Venus on a shell
facts.statement: Botticelli's The Birth of Venus shows the goddess arriving on a scallop shell, and hangs in the Uffizi in Florence.
facts.question: Which Botticelli painting shows Venus arriving on a scallop shell?

facts.title: The Dutch Mona Lisa
facts.statement: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring is not a portrait of a specific person but a tronie — a study of a type or expression.
facts.question: Which Vermeer painting is nicknamed 'the Dutch Mona Lisa'?

facts.title: The mural in Milan
facts.statement: Leonardo's The Last Supper is painted on a refectory wall in Milan. He used an experimental technique that began deteriorating within his lifetime.
facts.question: Which Leonardo mural in Milan shows Christ's final meal with the apostles?

facts.title: The farmer and the pitchfork
facts.statement: Grant Wood's American Gothic shows a farmer and his daughter — not his wife — in front of a Iowa farmhouse, and became an icon of rural America.
facts.question: Which painting shows a stern farmer holding a pitchfork beside a woman?

facts.title: The Spanish royal puzzle
facts.statement: Velázquez's Las Meninas plays games with perspective and the viewer's position, and is often called the greatest painting in the Prado.
facts.question: Which Velázquez painting depicts the Spanish royal household and the artist himself at work?

facts.title: Rembrandt's militia
facts.statement: Rembrandt's The Night Watch is not actually a night scene — centuries of darkened varnish gave it the name.
facts.question: Which Rembrandt group portrait of a militia company is misleadingly named for the night?
facts.hook: It was only 'night' because the varnish went brown.

facts.title: The ceiling in Rome
facts.statement: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512, standing on scaffolding rather than lying down as legend has it.
facts.question: Which ceiling did Michelangelo paint between 1508 and 1512?

facts.title: The polymath of Vinci
facts.statement: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, anatomist, engineer and inventor whose notebooks sketched flying machines centuries before flight.
facts.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?

facts.title: The painter who sold almost nothing
facts.statement: Vincent van Gogh produced around 2,100 artworks and sold very few in his lifetime; he died at 37 in relative obscurity.
facts.question: Who painted Sunflowers and The Starry Night?

facts.title: The co-founder of Cubism
facts.statement: Pablo Picasso co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque and produced an estimated 50,000 works across painting, sculpture and ceramics.
facts.question: Who co-founded Cubism and painted Guernica?

facts.title: The founder of Impressionism
facts.statement: Claude Monet gave Impressionism its name with his painting Impression, Sunrise, and painted his water-lily pond hundreds of times.
facts.question: Which painter's work Impression, Sunrise gave Impressionism its name?

facts.title: The Dutch master of light
facts.statement: Rembrandt van Rijn was the greatest painter of the Dutch Golden Age, famous for dramatic light and around 80 unflinching self-portraits.
facts.question: Which Dutch Golden Age painter produced around 80 self-portraits?

facts.title: Sculptor, painter, architect
facts.statement: Michelangelo considered himself primarily a sculptor, yet painted the Sistine Chapel and designed the dome of St Peter's Basilica.
facts.question: Who sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling?

facts.title: The Mexican self-portraitist
facts.statement: Frida Kahlo painted intensely personal self-portraits after a streetcar accident left her with lifelong pain.
facts.question: Which Mexican artist is known for intensely personal self-portraits?

facts.title: The Vienna gold period
facts.statement: Gustav Klimt's The Kiss, covered in gold leaf, is the defining work of his golden phase and of Viennese Art Nouveau.
facts.question: Which Austrian painter created The Kiss, covered in gold leaf?

facts.title: The drip painter
facts.statement: Jackson Pollock laid canvases on the floor and poured paint across them, making him the central figure of Abstract Expressionism.
facts.question: Which American painter created works by dripping and pouring paint onto canvases on the floor?

facts.title: The soup cans
facts.statement: Andy Warhol made Pop Art the dominant movement of the 1960s with silkscreens of Campbell's soup cans and Marilyn Monroe.
facts.question: Which artist made silkscreen prints of Campbell's soup cans?

facts.title: The Spanish surrealist
facts.statement: Salvador Dalí cultivated an eccentric public persona to match his meticulously rendered dream imagery.
facts.question: Which Spanish surrealist painted The Persistence of Memory?

facts.title: The Delft master
facts.statement: Johannes Vermeer produced only about 35 known paintings, most of them quiet domestic interiors lit from a window on the left.
facts.question: Which Dutch painter of quiet interiors left only about 35 known works?

facts.title: The English playwright
facts.statement: William Shakespeare wrote about 39 plays and 154 sonnets, and coined or popularised hundreds of English words still in use.
facts.question: Who wrote Hamlet, Macbeth and King Lear?

facts.title: The Russian epic novelist
facts.statement: Leo Tolstoy wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina, then renounced his own novels in favour of moral philosophy.
facts.question: Who wrote War and Peace?

facts.title: The Victorian serialist
facts.statement: Charles Dickens published most of his novels in monthly instalments, which is why they end so many chapters on a cliffhanger.
facts.question: Who wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations?

facts.title: The novelist of manners
facts.statement: Jane Austen published her novels anonymously, credited only as 'A Lady', and was not widely known as their author in her lifetime.
facts.question: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?

facts.title: The author of Big Brother
facts.statement: George Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four and Animal Farm; his real name was Eric Arthur Blair.
facts.question: Who wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four?

facts.title: The Greek epic poet
facts.statement: Homer is credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, the founding epics of Western literature, composed around the 8th century BC.
facts.question: Who is credited with composing the Iliad and the Odyssey?

facts.title: The first modern novel
facts.statement: Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615 and widely called the first modern novel.
facts.question: Who wrote Don Quixote?

facts.title: The writer who asked for his work to be burned
facts.statement: Franz Kafka instructed his friend Max Brod to destroy his unpublished manuscripts. Brod published them instead, giving us The Trial and The Castle.
facts.question: Which writer asked for his manuscripts to be burned, only for his friend to publish them?
facts.hook: We have The Trial only because someone ignored a dying man's instructions.

facts.title: The iceberg theory
facts.statement: Ernest Hemingway wrote in a spare, declarative style he called the iceberg theory, leaving most meaning beneath the surface.
facts.question: Who wrote The Old Man and the Sea?

facts.title: Magical realism
facts.statement: Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude brought magical realism to a world audience and won him the Nobel Prize.
facts.question: Who wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude?

facts.title: The psychologist of the novel
facts.statement: Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov after surviving a mock execution and four years in a Siberian prison camp.
facts.question: Who wrote Crime and Punishment?

facts.title: The stream of consciousness
facts.statement: Virginia Woolf pioneered stream-of-consciousness narration in Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse.
facts.question: Who wrote Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse?

facts.title: The Mississippi novelist
facts.statement: Mark Twain, born Samuel Clemens, wrote The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, which Hemingway called the source of all modern American literature.
facts.question: Who wrote The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn?

facts.title: The whale
facts.statement: Herman Melville's Moby-Dick sold poorly in his lifetime and was only recognised as a masterpiece decades after his death.
facts.question: Who wrote Moby-Dick?

facts.title: The Jazz Age novel
facts.statement: F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby sold modestly on release in 1925 and became a classic only after his death.
facts.question: Who wrote The Great Gatsby?

facts.title: The Napoleonic epic
facts.statement: War and Peace follows five aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of Russia across roughly 1,200 pages.
facts.question: Which Tolstoy novel follows Russian families through Napoleon's invasion?

facts.title: It is a truth universally acknowledged
facts.statement: Pride and Prejudice, published in 1813, follows Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy and opens with one of the most quoted lines in English.
facts.question: Which Jane Austen novel features Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy?

facts.title: The dystopia of surveillance
facts.statement: Nineteen Eighty-Four gave English the words doublethink, thoughtcrime and Big Brother.
facts.question: Which Orwell novel introduced Big Brother and doublethink?

facts.title: Tilting at windmills
facts.statement: Don Quixote follows an elderly gentleman who reads too many chivalric romances and sets out as a knight, mistaking windmills for giants.
facts.question: In which novel does the hero mistake windmills for giants?

facts.title: Call me Ishmael
facts.statement: Moby-Dick opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael' and follows Captain Ahab's obsessive hunt for a white whale.
facts.question: Which novel opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael'?

facts.title: The Buendía family
facts.statement: One Hundred Years of Solitude tells seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo.
facts.question: Which novel chronicles seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo?

facts.title: The murder and the conscience
facts.statement: Crime and Punishment follows the student Raskolnikov, who murders a pawnbroker and is destroyed by his own guilt rather than by the police.
facts.question: Which novel follows the student Raskolnikov after he murders a pawnbroker?

facts.title: The green light across the bay
facts.statement: The Great Gatsby is set on Long Island in 1922 and follows Jay Gatsby's pursuit of Daisy Buchanan.
facts.question: Which novel follows Jay Gatsby and the green light across the bay?

facts.title: One day in Dublin
facts.statement: James Joyce's Ulysses takes place over a single day, 16 June 1904, now celebrated annually as Bloomsday.
facts.question: Which novel takes place over a single day in Dublin, celebrated as Bloomsday?

facts.title: Atticus Finch
facts.statement: Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, published in 1960, won the Pulitzer Prize and was her only novel for 55 years.
facts.question: Which novel features the lawyer Atticus Finch defending Tom Robinson?

facts.title: The deaf composer
facts.statement: Ludwig van Beethoven continued composing after going deaf, writing the Ninth Symphony when he could no longer hear it performed.
facts.question: Which composer wrote his Ninth Symphony while completely deaf?
facts.hook: He had to be turned around at the premiere to see the audience applauding.

facts.title: The child prodigy
facts.statement: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was composing by five and toured Europe as a child, writing over 600 works before dying at 35.
facts.question: Which composer wrote The Magic Flute and died at 35?

facts.title: The Baroque master
facts.statement: Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the Brandenburg Concertos and the Mass in B minor, and was better known in his lifetime as an organist than a composer.
facts.question: Which Baroque composer wrote the Brandenburg Concertos?

facts.title: The ballet composer
facts.statement: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote Swan Lake, The Nutcracker and The Sleeping Beauty — the three pillars of classical ballet.
facts.question: Which composer wrote Swan Lake and The Nutcracker?

facts.title: The poet of the piano
facts.statement: Frédéric Chopin wrote almost exclusively for solo piano, and his heart is buried in Warsaw while his body lies in Paris.
facts.question: Which composer wrote almost exclusively for solo piano?

facts.title: The Red Priest
facts.statement: Antonio Vivaldi, an ordained priest nicknamed the Red Priest for his hair, wrote The Four Seasons and taught at a Venetian orphanage for girls.
facts.question: Which composer wrote The Four Seasons?

facts.title: The opera revolutionary
facts.statement: Richard Wagner wrote his own librettos and built his own theatre at Bayreuth to stage the four-opera Ring cycle.
facts.question: Which composer wrote the four-opera Ring cycle and built his own theatre?

facts.title: The Italian opera giant
facts.statement: Giuseppe Verdi wrote La traviata, Rigoletto and Aida, and became a symbol of Italian unification.
facts.question: Which composer wrote La traviata and Aida?

facts.title: The riot at the ballet
facts.statement: Igor Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring caused a near-riot at its 1913 Paris premiere with its violent rhythms and dissonance.
facts.question: Which composer's Rite of Spring caused a riot at its 1913 premiere?

facts.title: The Messiah
facts.statement: George Frideric Handel composed Messiah in just 24 days; its Hallelujah chorus is among the most performed works in Western music.
facts.question: Which composer wrote Messiah in about 24 days?

facts.title: Four violin concertos
facts.statement: The Four Seasons is a set of four violin concertos, each accompanied by a sonnet describing the season it depicts.
facts.question: Which Vivaldi work consists of four violin concertos, one per season?

facts.title: The Christmas ballet
facts.statement: The Nutcracker premiered in 1892 to lukewarm reviews and only became a Christmas institution decades later.
facts.question: Which Tchaikovsky ballet is a Christmas tradition worldwide?

facts.title: Fifteen hours of opera
facts.statement: Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen is a cycle of four operas lasting about fifteen hours, usually staged over four evenings.
facts.question: Which Wagner opera cycle lasts about fifteen hours across four evenings?

facts.title: Ode to Joy
facts.statement: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony was the first major symphony to use voices, setting Schiller's Ode to Joy — now the anthem of Europe.
facts.question: Which symphony sets Schiller's Ode to Joy and became the anthem of Europe?

facts.title: The ballet that caused a riot
facts.statement: The Rite of Spring depicts a pagan sacrificial ritual, and its 1913 premiere provoked shouting and fights in the audience.
facts.question: Which Stravinsky ballet depicts a pagan sacrificial rite?

facts.title: The Divine Comedy
facts.statement: Dante Alighieri wrote The Divine Comedy in Italian rather than Latin, helping establish Tuscan as the basis of modern Italian.
facts.question: Who wrote The Divine Comedy?

facts.title: The recluse of Amherst
facts.statement: Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems but published fewer than a dozen in her lifetime; the rest were found after her death.
facts.question: Which American poet wrote 1,800 poems but published almost none in her lifetime?

facts.title: Leaves of Grass
facts.statement: Walt Whitman self-published Leaves of Grass in 1855 and kept revising and expanding it for the rest of his life.
facts.question: Which American poet wrote and continually revised Leaves of Grass?

facts.title: The Waste Land
facts.statement: T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land, published in 1922, became the defining poem of literary modernism.
facts.question: Who wrote The Waste Land?

facts.title: The Persian mystic
facts.statement: Rumi, a 13th-century Persian poet and Sufi mystic, is among the most widely read poets in the world today.
facts.question: Which 13th-century Persian mystic is one of the world's most-read poets?

facts.title: The daffodils
facts.statement: William Wordsworth helped launch English Romanticism with Lyrical Ballads and wrote 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud'.
facts.question: Which Romantic poet wrote 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud'?

facts.title: The Cherry Orchard
facts.statement: Anton Chekhov wrote The Seagull, Uncle Vanya and The Cherry Orchard, and practised as a doctor throughout his writing life.
facts.question: Which Russian playwright wrote The Cherry Orchard and The Seagull?

facts.title: A Doll's House
facts.statement: Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House ended with a slammed door that scandalised 19th-century Europe and helped create modern drama.
facts.question: Which Norwegian playwright wrote A Doll's House?

facts.title: Waiting for Godot
facts.statement: Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot, in which nothing much happens twice, defined the Theatre of the Absurd.
facts.question: Who wrote Waiting for Godot?

facts.title: Oedipus Rex
facts.statement: Sophocles wrote Oedipus Rex and Antigone, and is said to have reduced the size of the Greek chorus while adding a third actor.
facts.question: Which ancient Greek playwright wrote Oedipus Rex?

facts.title: The Importance of Being Earnest
facts.statement: Oscar Wilde wrote one novel, several plays and a great many aphorisms, and was imprisoned at the height of his fame.
facts.question: Who wrote The Importance of Being Earnest?

facts.title: Tartuffe
facts.statement: Molière wrote Tartuffe and The Misanthrope, and collapsed on stage while performing in his own play about a hypochondriac.
facts.question: Which French playwright wrote Tartuffe?

facts.title: The marble giant in Florence
facts.statement: Michelangelo's David stands 5.17 m tall and was carved from a single block of marble that other sculptors had abandoned as flawed.
facts.question: Which Michelangelo sculpture depicts a biblical hero carved from a single marble block?

facts.title: The seated figure
facts.statement: Auguste Rodin's The Thinker was originally conceived as part of a larger work, The Gates of Hell, representing Dante.
facts.question: Which Rodin sculpture shows a seated man resting his chin on his hand?

facts.title: The armless goddess
facts.statement: The Venus de Milo, carved around 100 BC and now in the Louvre, was discovered on the Greek island of Milos in 1820.
facts.question: Which armless ancient Greek statue is displayed in the Louvre?

facts.title: The winged figure on the stairs
facts.statement: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, a Hellenistic statue of Nike, stands at the top of the Louvre's Daru staircase.
facts.question: Which headless winged statue stands atop a grand staircase in the Louvre?

facts.title: The statue above Rio
facts.statement: Christ the Redeemer, completed in 1931, stands 30 m tall atop Corcovado mountain overlooking Rio de Janeiro.
facts.question: Which statue overlooks Rio de Janeiro from Corcovado mountain?

facts.title: The house over a waterfall
facts.statement: Frank Lloyd Wright designed Fallingwater, cantilevered directly over a waterfall in Pennsylvania, and the spiral Guggenheim Museum.
facts.question: Which architect designed Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum in New York?

facts.title: The unfinished basilica
facts.statement: Antoni Gaudí designed the Sagrada Família in Barcelona, begun in 1882 and still unfinished today.
facts.question: Which architect designed the Sagrada Família in Barcelona?
facts.hook: Under construction for over 140 years and counting.

facts.title: The machine for living in
facts.statement: Le Corbusier defined a house as 'a machine for living in' and shaped 20th-century modernist architecture and urban planning.
facts.question: Which architect called a house 'a machine for living in'?

facts.title: The queen of the curve
facts.statement: Zaha Hadid was the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize, known for sweeping, curvilinear buildings.
facts.question: Who was the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize?

facts.title: The iron tower
facts.statement: Gustave Eiffel's tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair and was meant to be dismantled after twenty years.
facts.question: Which engineer designed the tower built for the 1889 Paris World's Fair?
facts.hook: Paris nearly tore it down — it survived because it made a good radio mast.

facts.title: Painting the light
facts.statement: Impressionism emerged in 1870s France, using visible brushstrokes and outdoor painting to capture changing light rather than precise detail.
facts.question: Which art movement sought to capture fleeting light with visible brushstrokes in 1870s France?

facts.title: Objects from every angle at once
facts.statement: Cubism, developed by Picasso and Braque around 1907, fractured objects into geometric planes shown from several viewpoints simultaneously.
facts.question: Which movement broke objects into geometric planes seen from multiple viewpoints at once?

facts.title: The art of dreams
facts.statement: Surrealism, launched by André Breton's 1924 manifesto, drew on dreams and the unconscious to produce irrational imagery.
facts.question: Which movement drew on dreams and the unconscious, launched by a 1924 manifesto?

facts.title: The rebirth
facts.statement: The Renaissance began in 14th-century Italy, reviving classical learning and producing Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael.
facts.question: Which cultural movement began in 14th-century Italy and revived classical learning?

facts.title: Drama and grandeur
facts.statement: Baroque art of the 17th century used dramatic light, movement and emotional intensity, in painters like Caravaggio and Rubens.
facts.question: Which 17th-century movement used dramatic light and emotional intensity?

facts.title: Feeling over accuracy
facts.statement: Expressionism distorted form and colour to convey emotional experience rather than physical reality, centred in early 20th-century Germany.
facts.question: Which movement distorted colour and form to convey emotion over physical reality?
